Which number are you reporting?

Source: vignettes/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd
library(mysterymodel)

A clinical prediction paper reports a c-statistic. There are at least four different quantities with that name available from one fitted model, they differ by more than the rounding a manuscript shows, and nothing in the number itself says which one it is. mm_validate() returns all of them, one per row, labelled, so that choosing is a decision someone makes rather than a default nobody noticed.

cohort <- mm_synthetic_cohort(n = 600, prevalence = 0.11, seed = 1978)

project <- mm_project("uds", "event",
                      c("age", "bmi", "sex", "prior_uti"),
                      positive_class = 1, cohort = cohort,
                      split_var = "year", split_at = 2023,
                      cluster_id = "pid", seed = 1978)

model <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_model(project, cohort, nonlinear = "age",
           interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex"))))

validation <- mm_validate(model, cohort, B = 100, full_process = TRUE)
validation$metrics[, c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "cal_slope",
                       "brier")]
#>                     basis   n events    c_stat cal_slope      brier
#> 1                apparent 404     45 0.6647478        NA 0.09391697
#> 2  bootstrap, fixed model 404     45 0.6067696 0.7126282         NA
#> 3 bootstrap, full process 404     45 0.6065333 0.7074585 0.09828239
#> 4                held out 196     22 0.7857889 1.7369817 0.08482979

The four bases

Apparent is the model scored on the rows it was fitted to. It is always optimistic, and it is reported here so that the optimism is visible rather than absent.

Bootstrap, fixed model comes from rms::validate(). Each resample refits the same formula, which corrects the optimism of estimating coefficients. It re-derives nothing the formula was shaped by.

Bootstrap, full process refits the whole strategy inside every resample: knot placement, datadist and factor-level handling are all learned from the resample rather than inherited from the original fit.

Held out is the rows the project’s split reserved, scored once.

Two cells are empty, for two different reasons, and both are the right answer.

The brier cell on the fixed-model row is empty because rms::validate() returns Somers’ Dxy and the calibration slope, not a Brier score. Carrying the apparent Brier across into that row would make it look corrected when nothing corrected it.

The scaled Brier gets the same treatment one step further on. It is a score against a reference, and left alone each basis would use its own prevalence, so a column of them would be scores against different references. Every basis here is scaled against the development cohort’s reference, reported as brier_ref, and a basis with a prevalence of its own keeps that value in its note:

validation$metrics[, c("basis", "brier", "brier_ref", "brier_scaled")]
#>                     basis      brier  brier_ref brier_scaled
#> 1                apparent 0.09391697 0.09897927  0.051144980
#> 2  bootstrap, fixed model         NA         NA           NA
#> 3 bootstrap, full process 0.09828239 0.09897927  0.007040662
#> 4                held out 0.08482979 0.09897927  0.142953979

The cal_slope cell on the apparent row is empty because that number is an identity rather than an estimate. Scoring an unpenalized maximum-likelihood fit on the very rows that produced it forces the calibration intercept to zero and the slope to one: they are the fit’s own score equations rearranged. Printed beside a held-out slope they read as the model being perfectly calibrated, which is the one thing they cannot show. You can watch them be exactly that:

y <- as.integer(model$fit$y)
lp <- as.numeric(model$fit$linear.predictors)
c(intercept = unname(coef(glm(y ~ 1, family = binomial(), offset = lp))[1]),
  slope     = unname(coef(glm(y ~ lp, family = binomial()))[2]))
#>    intercept        slope 
#> 8.172466e-17 1.000000e+00

The package detects the identity rather than assuming it, so a fitting method that does not force it, a penalized fit for instance, would have its apparent calibration reported as the estimate it would then be.

parts <- mysterymodel:::mm_split(project, cohort)
c(development = nrow(parts$dev), held_out = nrow(parts$held))
#> development    held_out 
#>         404         196
range(parts$dev$year)
#> [1] 2019 2022
range(parts$held$year)
#> [1] 2023 2024

One function owns the split, so fitting, validation and held-out scoring cannot disagree about which rows are development. A row with a missing year falls on neither side, and is an error rather than a silent drop.

What the full process does and does not cover

This is the distinction the package will not let a caller skip. The detail object names what was actually repeated:

detail <- validation$full_process_detail
detail$covers
#> [1] "knot placement" "datadist"       "factor levels"
cat(detail$note, "\n")
#> full-process bootstrap, 100 of 100 resamples valid. Re-derives knots, datadist and factor levels per resample; imputation, selection and tuning are not in this pipeline yet. Resampled by whole pid. The correction is a mean over resamples and carries a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.00441 on the c-statistic and 0.02021 on the slope, so these figures are determined to about 2 decimal place(s) and not to as many as they print with

covers is a list that will grow. Imputation, selection, tuning and interaction screening are not re-executed, because the package does not do them yet. A strategy including any of them is not fully validated by this function either, and saying so in the returned object is what keeps the claim honest as the pipeline grows.

The optimism and the correction are both available, rather than only their difference:

round(rbind(apparent  = unlist(detail$apparent[names(detail$optimism)]),
            optimism  = detail$optimism,
            corrected = detail$corrected), 4)
#>           c_stat cal_intercept cal_slope   brier brier_scaled
#> apparent  0.6647             0    1.0000  0.0939       0.0511
#> optimism  0.0582             0    0.2925 -0.0044       0.0441
#> corrected 0.6065             0    0.7075  0.0983       0.0070

Those two calibration numbers in the apparent row are the identity again, and here they are load bearing rather than misleading: an in-sample slope that is exactly one in every resample is what makes the optimism of the slope equal to the mean out-of-sample shortfall, which is the quantity the corrected row reports.

The scaled Brier in that table is derived, not differenced. It divides by rate * (1 - rate) of whichever rows were scored, so an in-sample value and an out-of-sample value are scaled by different constants and their difference would carry that drift as well as the optimism. The Brier itself is on one scale throughout, so it is corrected and the scaled version is then computed from the corrected value against one fixed denominator, the development cohort’s own no-information Brier:

c(no_information_brier = detail$no_information_brier,
  corrected_brier      = unname(detail$corrected[["brier"]]),
  derived_scaled       = unname(detail$corrected[["brier_scaled"]]),
  check = 1 - unname(detail$corrected[["brier"]]) /
    detail$no_information_brier)
#> no_information_brier      corrected_brier       derived_scaled 
#>          0.098979267          0.098282387          0.007040662 
#>                check 
#>          0.007040662

On a cohort of 150 that correction moved the reported number from -0.024 to -0.040, so it is not a rounding matter.

Resamples that cannot be fitted are counted, not dropped quietly:

c(valid = detail$valid, of = detail$B)
#> valid    of 
#>   100   100
detail$adequate
#> [1] TRUE
detail$failures
#> character(0)

A resample that separates, or that is missing a factor level, is a real feature of a small cohort. An optimism averaged over the survivors of a selection nobody reported is not the quantity it claims to be, so the count is part of the result and adequate is FALSE when too few fitted.

One caution about comparing the two bootstrap rows

They look comparable and are not. The fixed-model row derives its c-statistic from rms‘s Somers’ Dxy as 0.5 + Dxy / 2; the full-process row is a mean of pROC AUCs over resamples. Two estimators of the same population quantity differ a little by construction, so a small gap between those two rows carries no information about the modelling strategy. Compare each against apparent, which is the comparison each was built to support.

Resampling the patient rather than the row

The cohort has repeat visits. Resampling rows treats two visits by one person as two independent facts, and that narrows every interval it touches.

dev <- parts$dev
by_row     <- mysterymodel:::mm_resample(dev, cluster_id = NULL)
by_patient <- mysterymodel:::mm_resample(dev, cluster_id = "pid")

c(rows_in_cohort = nrow(dev),
  row_draw       = length(by_row),
  patient_draw   = length(by_patient))
#> rows_in_cohort       row_draw   patient_draw 
#>            404            404            405

A row draw always has exactly as many rows as the cohort. A patient draw has as many patients, so its row count varies with which patients were drawn, and a patient contributing two visits brings both or neither.

Here is the property that matters, stated as a check rather than as a claim. Take the patients with exactly two visits, and count how many rows each of them contributes to the draw:

drawn <- dev[by_patient, ]
twins <- names(which(table(dev$pid) == 2L))
rows_drawn <- table(factor(drawn$pid, levels = twins))

table(rows_drawn %% 2L)
#> 
#>  0 
#> 22
range(rows_drawn)
#> [1] 0 4

Every count is even. A patient drawn once brings two rows, a patient drawn twice brings four, a patient not drawn brings none. No single visit is ever separated from its sibling, which is what makes the resample a draw of patients rather than a draw of rows wearing patient labels.

The project declares cluster_id = "pid", so both bootstraps draw patients:

validation$clustered_by
#> [1] "pid"
validation$fixed_model$clustered_by
#> [1] "pid"

That second one was this package’s own omission for a while, and the note used to blame rms for it. rms::validate() passes its extra arguments through to rms::predab.resample(), which takes a cluster and draws whole units when it is given one, so nothing but the missing argument was stopping it.

cat(strwrap(validation$metrics$note[validation$metrics$basis ==
                                    "bootstrap, fixed model"], 72), sep = "\n")
#> rms::validate, 100 of 100 resample(s) fitted. Refits the same formula;
#> does not re-derive knots or levels. Resampled by whole pid. No
#> interval: DeLong describes an apparent c-statistic, not a corrected
#> one, and an interval for the corrected index needs a nested bootstrap
#> that is not implemented here

The resample count in that note is the number rms actually fitted, not the number asked for. predab.resample() keeps only the resamples that converged and mentions the shortfall only when pr = TRUE, which validate.lrm leaves off, so a corrected index can be an average over the resamples that happened to work with nothing on the object to say so. The count comes back as the n column, and falling below four fifths of B is reported as inadequate, the same threshold the full-process row uses.

Scoring any set of predictions

The metric helper that produces each row is usable on its own, which is how a calibration or subgroup table gets the same arithmetic as the main table instead of a second implementation of it:

y <- mysterymodel:::mm_event_indicator(parts$held$event, 1)
p <- mm_predict(model, parts$held)$.pred

by_hand <- mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(p, y, basis = "held out, by hand")
by_hand[, c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "c_lower", "c_upper",
            "cal_intercept", "cal_slope")]
#>               basis   n events    c_stat   c_lower   c_upper cal_intercept
#> 1 held out, by hand 196     22 0.7857889 0.6770106 0.8945672   -0.05204503
#>   cal_slope
#> 1  1.736982

Those are the same numbers as the held-out row of the main table, because it is the same function. One column is deliberately not the same, and it is worth seeing why:

held_row <- validation$metrics[validation$metrics$basis == "held out", ]
c(main_table   = held_row$brier_scaled,
  main_ref     = held_row$brier_ref,
  by_hand      = by_hand$brier_scaled,
  by_hand_ref  = by_hand$brier_ref)
#>  main_table    main_ref     by_hand by_hand_ref 
#>  0.14295398  0.09897927  0.14868833  0.09964598

A scaled Brier is a score against a reference, and a bare call uses the reference of the rows it was given. The main table passes the development cohort’s reference to every basis instead, so that reading down the column compares like with like. A subgroup table wants the bare behaviour, since each subgroup’s own skill score is the question being asked there.

By subgroup 

held <- parts$held
held$.p <- p
held$.y <- y

do.call(rbind, lapply(split(held, held$sex), function(g)
  mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(g$.p, g$.y, basis = as.character(g$sex[1]))[
    , c("basis", "n", "events", "c_stat", "cal_slope")]))
#>         basis   n events    c_stat cal_slope
#> female female 142     11 0.6932686  1.421728
#> male     male  54     11 0.8456660  2.062632

Read those with the event counts beside them. A c-statistic from a few dozen events is compatible with a wide range of truths, and the interval columns are in the full return value for exactly that reason.

What the interval is, and the three rows that do not have one

The interval on a c-statistic is DeLong’s, from pROC, and it describes the c-statistic of one model scored once on one sample. Two of the four rows in the table above are not that.

validation$metrics[, c("basis", "n", "events", "non_events",
                       "c_stat", "c_lower", "c_upper")]
#>                     basis   n events non_events    c_stat   c_lower   c_upper
#> 1                apparent 404     45        359 0.6647478 0.5749341 0.7545614
#> 2  bootstrap, fixed model 404     45        359 0.6067696        NA        NA
#> 3 bootstrap, full process 404     45        359 0.6065333        NA        NA
#> 4                held out 196     22        174 0.7857889 0.6770106 0.8945672

The bootstrap rows carry no interval, and the reason is in their notes rather than left as a pair of blanks:

cat(strwrap(validation$metrics$note[
  validation$metrics$basis == "bootstrap, fixed model"], 72), sep = "\n")
#> rms::validate, 100 of 100 resample(s) fitted. Refits the same formula;
#> does not re-derive knots or levels. Resampled by whole pid. No
#> interval: DeLong describes an apparent c-statistic, not a corrected
#> one, and an interval for the corrected index needs a nested bootstrap
#> that is not implemented here

A corrected index is an apparent one minus an average optimism. Neither rms::validate() nor the full-process loop returns the distribution of that difference, so there is nothing to put an interval around; the recognised answer is a nested bootstrap, which costs B times the correction and is not implemented here. What must not happen is the apparent row’s interval being read down the column as though it applied to the corrected estimate, which is why the blanks are annotated.

Two more cases are reported rather than hidden. DeLong needs at least two of each outcome, so a cohort with one event gets its c-statistic and no interval:

one_event <- mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(
  c(0.9, seq(0.1, 0.5, length.out = 40)), c(1, rep(0, 40)),
  basis = "one event")
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
one_event[, c("n", "events", "non_events", "c_stat", "c_lower")]
#>    n events non_events c_stat c_lower
#> 1 41      1         40      1      NA
cat(strwrap(one_event$note, 72), sep = "\n")
#> the c-statistic has no interval here, which needs at least two of each
#> outcome, and there are 1 event(s) and 40 non-event(s). the calibration
#> slope is withheld: the fit behind it did not converge, so its
#> coefficient marks where iteration stopped rather than an estimate

And where the classes separate completely, DeLong’s standard error is zero, so the interval it returns has zero width. That is the estimator running out of information, not a precise answer, and the note says so rather than leaving 1.000 to 1.000 on the page:

separated <- mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(
  c(seq(0, 0.4, length.out = 30), seq(0.6, 1, length.out = 30)),
  rep(0:1, each = 30), basis = "separated")
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge
#> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
cat(strwrap(separated$note, 72), sep = "\n")
#> 95% DeLong interval, from 30 event(s) and 30 non-event(s). that
#> interval has zero width, which is what DeLong returns when the classes
#> separate completely or every prediction ties: the estimator has no
#> information left to spend on an interval, so this is not a statement of
#> precision. the calibration slope is withheld: the fit behind it did not
#> converge, so its coefficient marks where iteration stopped rather than
#> an estimate

No threshold on the event count is applied anywhere in this. There is no evidence in this package for a universal minimum, so instead every row states the method and the two counts its standard error is computed from, and a reader judges the three-event interval for themselves.

Rows that cannot be judged

The cohort above is complete. A real external cohort is not, and the two ways it is incomplete are not the same thing.

holey <- cohort
held_rows <- which(holey$year >= 2023)
holey$bmi[1:25] <- NA                      # development, a missing predictor
holey$bmi[held_rows[1:9]] <- NA            # external, a missing predictor
holey$event[held_rows[20:27]] <- NA        # external, a missing outcome
holey$bmi[held_rows[26:30]] <- NA          # and the overlap of the two

holey_model <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_model(project, holey, nonlinear = "age",
           interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex"))))
holey_validation <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_validate(holey_model, holey, B = 50, full_process = TRUE))

holey_validation
#> <mm_validation>  full-process: TRUE
#>   columns: n, events/non-events, c-statistic with its 95% DeLong interval where one is estimable
#>   apparent                 n=389   43/346 C=0.6605 (0.5669-0.7541)
#>   bootstrap, fixed model   n=389   43/346 C=0.5894 no interval, see note  slope=0.6522
#>   bootstrap, full process  n=389   43/346 C=0.5971 no interval, see note  slope=0.6921
#>   held out                 n=175   19/156 C=0.7702 (0.6491-0.8914)  slope=1.6426
#>   development eligibility: 389 of 404 scored, 15 missing a predictor, 0 missing the outcome, 0 both
#>   held out eligibility: 175 of 196 scored, 13 missing a predictor, 6 missing the outcome, 2 both
#>   Full process re-derives knot placement, datadist, factor levels per resample; 50 of 50 valid.
#>   Its correction carries a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.00632 on C; rms does not return
#>   the per-resample values its own row is averaged over, so the
#>   same figure cannot be given for the fixed-model row.
str(holey_validation$eligibility$held_out)
#> List of 7
#>  $ n_total          : int 196
#>  $ n_scored         : int 175
#>  $ n_excluded       : int 21
#>  $ missing_predictor: int 13
#>  $ missing_outcome  : int 6
#>  $ missing_both     : int 2
#>  $ by_variable      : Named int [1:2] 15 8
#>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:2] "bmi" "event"

A patient missing a predictor cannot be scored. A patient missing the outcome can be scored but contributes nothing to a performance estimate. They are counted apart, with the overlap separately, because collapsing them hides which and because the specific error worth preventing is quietly taking a missing outcome for a non-event: that leaves the event count unchanged while inflating the denominator, so every reported risk comes out low and nothing in the table looks wrong.

held <- holey[holey$year >= 2023, ]
row <- holey_validation$metrics[holey_validation$metrics$basis == "held out", ]
c(rows_in_the_held_out_period = nrow(held),
  rows_scored                 = row$n,
  events_among_them           = row$events)
#> rows_in_the_held_out_period                 rows_scored 
#>                         196                         175 
#>           events_among_them 
#>                          19

The bootstraps resample the fitted cohort and not the frame it was handed, so a resample’s composition does not depend on how much of it was missing:

c(supplied = holey_model$n_supplied,
  fitted   = holey_model$n_dev,
  resampled_by_the_full_process =
    holey_validation$full_process_detail$eligibility$n_scored)
#>                      supplied                        fitted 
#>                           404                           389 
#> resampled_by_the_full_process 
#>                           389

And the caveat travels with the number rather than living in a methods section:

cat(strwrap(row$note, 72), sep = "\n")
#> year >= 2023, scored once. 175 of 196 row(s) scored, 21 excluded (13
#> for a missing predictor, 6 for a missing outcome, 2 for both; bmi 15,
#> event 8). Complete case, so these estimates assume the exclusions are
#> uninformative, which is an assumption and not a finding. 95% DeLong
#> interval, from 19 event(s) and 156 non-event(s). the scaled Brier is
#> taken against the reference 0.09832, not this sample's own 0.09678, so
#> the column compares like with like; against its own it would read
#> 0.1370

That last sentence is the point. Complete-case analysis is a computational strategy, not a guarantee. Missingness can be informative, the more so in a cohort this size, so the exclusions are disclosed everywhere they apply instead of being summarised away. Multiple imputation is the answer and is not in this package yet; mm_predict() keeps refusing to put a number on an incomplete record in the meantime.

Two input contracts

A bootstrap count is a count. B = 2.7 used to run two resamples, which answers a question nobody asked, so it is refused along with NA, NaN, either infinity, a vector, a string and anything below one. A count written with a decimal point is still a count, so 200.0 is fine. The check runs before any seed is set, so a refused call leaves the random-number state as it found it.

mm_validate(model, cohort, B = 2.7)
#> Error:
#> ! `B` is 2.7, which is not a whole number of resamples. Truncating it to 2 would answer a question that was not asked.

A predicted probability is a probability. mm_metrics() used to clamp its input to the interior of [0, 1], so a predicted risk of 1.5 became a Brier score of 0.18 and whatever produced the 1.5 stayed invisible.

mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(c(1.5, 0.4, 0.6), c(1L, 0L, 1L), basis = "probe")
#> Error:
#> ! predicted probabilities must be finite and within [0, 1]. Found 1 invalid value(s); row 1 is 1.5.

Zero and one are valid probabilities. Their logits are infinite and the calibration terms are fitted on the logit scale, so a nudge survives on that one line and nowhere else: the Brier and the c-statistic read the probabilities as given.

edge <- mysterymodel:::mm_metrics(c(0, 1, 0.4, 0.6), c(0L, 1L, 1L, 0L),
                                  basis = "probe")
c(brier_reported = edge$brier,
  brier_by_hand  = mean((c(0, 1, 0.4, 0.6) - c(0L, 1L, 1L, 0L))^2),
  slope_estimable = !is.na(edge$cal_slope))
#>  brier_reported   brier_by_hand slope_estimable 
#>            0.18            0.18            1.00

The honest summary

A fingerprint ties a validation result to the fit that produced it, so a table cannot drift from its model without the pairing changing:

identical(validation$fingerprint, model$fingerprint)
#> [1] TRUE
substr(validation$fingerprint, 1, 16)
#> [1] "92df44fff5c5dae3"

Report the held-out row when a split exists, the full-process row when it does not, the apparent row beside either so the optimism is visible, and the note column verbatim in the supplement.
